title: The Playboy of the Western World
wpTitle: Reviews of The Playboy of the Western World at the National Theatre starring Nicola Coughlan, Siobhán McSweeney & Éanna Hardwicke

A strong turn from Nicola Coughlan … The Bridgerton star plays a feisty barmaid in this revival of JM Synge’s 1907 comedy that once caused riots … It’s a great coup for the National Theatre to have tempted Nicola Coughlan back to the stage from the stellar televisual orbit to which Derry Girls and especially Bridgerton have propelled her … ... the portrayal of poverty and repressed lasciviousness that caused riots when the play originally opened at Dublin’s Abbey Theatre now feel quaint and stereotypical. … Hardwick’s stylised, child-like performance as Christy, and Coughlan’s more naturalistic one... are the strongest aspects of this revival by Catrionia McLaughlin, the Abbey’s current artistic director. Nicola Coughlan serves comedy and tragedy in pub drama … Coughlan plays a barmaid, alongside Derry Girls co-star Siobhán McSweeney, in JM Synge’s 1907 classic … This revival by the Abbey’s current artistic director, Caitríona McLaughlin, makes clear that it is something of a woman’s play, ahead of its time, with two female leads abjuring conservative Catholic morality to hope for something bigger than a small, scratching country existence. … ... there are bumpy transitions between the drama of the first half, with a subtly twisting tension and notes of anxiety, to the physical comedy and outright farce of the second. … Staged in its original, melodic Hiberno-English dialect, it is authentic but hard to follow at times, at least for this critic. … Synge could even have been the Tarantino of

An assured turn from Nicola Coughlan … The Bridgerton star is a standout in JM Synge’s play, alongside Derry Girls alumna Siobhán McSweeney, but this National Theatre staging misses the text’s dark humour … [Nicola Coughlan] gives an assured performance as a wilful young woman who falls under the spell of Christy Mahon … But be warned: this production from Caitríona McLaughlin, the artistic director of the Abbey Theatre in Dublin, is too reverential to do full justice to the dark humour in the text. Nicola Coughlan leads a gorgeous but uneven production … JM Synge’s 1907 Irish tragicomedy captures a community’s ravening hunger for something new … Two of Ireland’s best-loved comic actors go head to head in this moody staging of a neglected 1907 farce. Nicola Coughlan (Bridgerton, Derry Girls) and Siobhán McSweeney (Derry Girls) are armoured in corsets and many-layered skirts, fighting over the same man – the title’s Playboy. … JM Synge’s landmark Irish tragicomedy is a singular exploration of mass hysteria, female sexuality and mob rule. Bridgerton’s Nicola Coughlan can’t save this inaudible Irish classic … The National ought to have resolved the inaccessibility of JM Synge’s poetry before staging The Playboy of the Western World … Nicola Coughlan, of Derry Girls and Bridgerton fame, is the main draw for this revival of JM Synge’s once scandalous 1907 oddity … ... the National’s production is hampered by an avoidable problem: thanks to the use of archaic Irish accents and syntax, Synge’s succulent poetry is frequently unintelligible – almost to the point of inaccessible – to those not acquainted with the dialect. … In Caitriona McLaughlin’s staging, it becomes partly a comedy of repressed female desire. … You can trace a direct line between Synge’s lurid farce, the existential comedy of Beckett and the queasy closeness bet

Appealingly edgy and unsettling … Strong performances from Nicola Coughlan and Declan Conlon hold together this uneven, oddly paced study of rural insularity … It might feel innocuous now, but Abbey Theatre director Caitriona McLaughlin still gives this revival an appealingly edgy, unsettling treatment. … McLaughlin pitches the piece somewhere between slow-building farce and folk horror, with lies and misunderstandings gradually piling up over the course of long, directionless conversations until the characters collapse under their weight. … Katie Davenport’s striking design work elevates the production. … It looks great; bleak and vivid and just slightly disconcerting. It’s not just that the poetic, scattershot Irish classic is staged by Dublin Abbey Theatre’s Caitríona McLaughlin and designed by her visionary collaborator Katie Davenport, her work here painterly and gorgeous. … Nicola Coughlan as publican’s daughter Pegeen Mike, obsessed with titular playboy Christy Mahon (Éanna Hardwicke, terrific) until she gets his measure followed by her vengeance, is a luscious, complex but frustrated woman … Hardwicke’s surprisingly fragile Christy is no swaggering charmer, more a bewildered kid who can’t quite believe he’s become the centre of so much attention. … Honestly, Synge’s text, delivered with immaculate fidelity to a very specific dialect, is challenging to anybody not au fait with the vernacular of early 20th century County Mayo. … There’s little drama
